- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Without `limit` you get at most 2000 lines from the start of the file. When you already know which part you need, read only that part; this matters most for large files.

- A directory, a path that does not exist or an empty file gives an error or a note instead of content.

- Commit or push only when the user asks; on the default branch, create a branch first.
- When an attribution reminder is present, close every commit message and pull request description with its lines.

description.description:
What the command does, in plain words and the active voice, for a user who reads this without seeing the command: do not repeat the command, its flags or its paths, and do not use the words "complex" or "risk".

A simple command gets about 5-10 words:
- pytest -q -> "Run the test suite"
- git log -5 -> "Show the five latest commits"
- make build -> "Build the package"

A pipeline or an unusual flag gets enough context to be understood:
- du -sh * | sort -h | tail -3 -> "Show which three folders here use the most disk"
- docker ps -q | xargs docker stop -> "Stop every running container"
- tar -xzf release.tgz -C out -> "Unpack the release archive into the out folder"

- Read the file in this conversation before editing it; otherwise the edit fails.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, indentation included, and occur only once; otherwise the edit fails. Add surrounding lines to make it unique, or set `replace_all`.
- Leave out Read's line prefix (the number and the tab after it) when you copy text into `old_string` or `new_string`.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence, for example to rename something throughout the file.

Reads one file from the local filesystem: text, an image, a PDF or a Jupyter notebook.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Without `limit` you get at most 2000 lines from the start of the file. When you already know which part you need, read only that part; this matters most for large files.
- Lines come back numbered like `cat -n`, starting at 1.
- Images (PNG, JPG and the like) are shown to you as images.
- PDFs are read through `pages`, at most 20 pages per call; a PDF longer than 10 pages needs `pages`.
- Notebooks (`.ipynb`) come back as their cells, with their outputs.
- A directory, a path that does not exist or an empty file gives an error or a note instead of content.
- Do not read a file again just to check an edit you made: a failed Edit or Write reports an error, and the file's state is tracked for you.

Recall original messages that compaction collapsed into the summary note at the head of the conversation.

The originals are retained in full — the note merely stands in for them in the prompt. Use this tool when the note lacks a detail you need: the exact text of an earlier error, code you produced or discussed before compaction, or the precise wording of an earlier exchange. The collapsed range is [0, boundary); the current boundary is reported in every result and in the collapsed-context reminder.

Results are a read-only rendering of the original messages; long blocks are truncated with a marker. Page through a large range with repeated calls, advancing `offset`.

tools.description:
Launch a sub-agent to handle a focused, self-contained task and get its result back.

## What it does

Spawns one sub-agent per call: pick a `subagent_type` from the roster, give it the full task as `prompt`, and label it with a short `description` (3–5 words, shown to the user). The agent works in its own context and returns its final text as this call's result; that text is NOT shown to the user, so relay what matters.

**Parallelism**: emit SEVERAL Task calls in ONE assistant turn — they run CONCURRENTLY and their results come back together. Issuing one Task per turn is strictly sequential; when work is independent, always batch the calls into a single turn.

Once you have delegated a piece of work, do not also do it yourself — wait for the result and build on it.

## When to use

- The task fits a sub-agent type: a read-only scout for broad searches, a general-purpose worker for a self-contained coding task, an architect for a plan.
- Delegating independent work keeps your own context clean, or the answer means sweeping many files and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps.

## When NOT to use

- A single-fact lookup where you already know the file or symbol — just look it up yourself.
- Work that needs your accumulated conversation context — a sub-agent starts fresh and sees ONLY its `prompt`, so make the prompt self-contained: the goal, the constraints, and what to return.
tools.name: Task

background.description: Run the sub-agent in the background instead of waiting for it. With background=true you immediately get a 'started' acknowledgement and keep working; the sub-agent runs concurrently and its result is delivered to you automatically when it finishes — you never poll or wait. Use it for independent, longer-running work (research, a broad scan) you want off the critical path. Omit it (the default) to delegate and wait for the result inline. Only valid on a turn with exactly ONE Task call (a parallel batch is always foreground).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task.

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform.

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task. Available: explore — Read-only scout: fans out (glob/grep/read + read-only shell) to investigate the workspace and report facts (never edits).; general-purpose — General-purpose worker for self-contained coding tasks: search, read, write, edit, run shell commands, then return the result.; plan — Architect: reads the code and returns a concrete ordered implementation plan (read-only — never writes any file).

tools.description:
Use this tool to create and manage a structured task list for the current session.

## When to use

- Complex multi-step work (roughly three or more distinct steps), or the user handed you several tasks at once.
- Mark a todo `in_progress` BEFORE you start it and `completed` the moment it is fully done — keep exactly ONE item `in_progress` at a time.
- Update the list in real time as work lands; you may batch a TodoWrite with file, search and shell calls, or with `Task` calls, in the same response — not with `AskUserQuestion` or `skill`, which go on their own.

## When NOT to use

- A single, straightforward step, or a purely conversational / informational request — the bookkeeping overhead is not worth it.

## Shape

A call replaces the entire list — always send the FULL list, never a delta; omitting an item deletes it. Each item is `{content, status, activeForm}`: `content` in imperative form ("Run tests"), `status` one of `pending` / `in_progress` / `completed`, `activeForm` in present-continuous form ("Running tests"), shown while the item is in progress.

Only mark `completed` when the item truly succeeded; if it is blocked, errored, or tests still fail, keep it `in_progress` and add a follow-up item.
tools.name: TodoWrite

todos.description: The full checklist (replace-all). Each item: {content, status, activeForm}.

activeForm.description: Present-continuous form shown while in_progress, e.g. 'Running tests'.

content.description: Imperative form of the task, e.g. 'Run tests'.

tools.description:
Fetch the full definition of deferred tools so you can call them.

Some tools are deferred: only their names are listed, in a message in this conversation, and their parameter schemas are not loaded. Calling a deferred tool before loading it fails. Pass a query here; the tools it matches are loaded, and from then on you call each one directly by its own name, exactly like the tools defined at the start. A loaded tool stays available for the rest of the conversation.

The matched definitions come back in the same encoding as the tool list you started with: one <function>{"description": ..., "name": ..., "parameters": ...}</function> line per tool, inside a <functions> block.

Ways to query:
- "select:WebFetch,NotebookEdit" loads exactly the named tools
- "fetch url page" searches names and descriptions and loads up to max_results best matches
- "+mcp resource" keeps only tools whose name contains "mcp", ranked by the other words
tools.name: ToolSearch

max_results.description: The most tools a keyword search loads (default 5).

query.description: Which tools to load: "select:<name>[,<name>...]" for exact names, otherwise keywords to search for.

tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to Markdown, and answers `prompt` against it — returning the answer, not the raw page.

- `http(s)` URLs only. A logged-in URL answers 401/403 (or is unreachable) and the call fails with the cause named — don't retry those.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Fetched pages are cached for 15 minutes per URL, so a follow-up `prompt` about the same page is cheap.
- To search the web rather than fetch a known page, use `WebSearch`.

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

Writes a file, replacing it if it already exists.

- Use it to create a file, or to replace one you have read in full.
- Overwriting an existing file that you have not read in this conversation fails.
- To change part of a file, use Edit.
tools.name: Write

content.description: The whole content of the file.

file_path.description: Absolute path of the file to write (an absolute path, not a relative one).

tools.description: Retire an outdated or superseded memory: move it into the memory directory's archive/ subdirectory, removing it from the index, recall and search. Nothing is ever deleted — a human can restore the file from archive/.
tools.name: memory_archive

name.description: Memory name as listed in the memory index.

tools.description: Load the full markdown body of a named memory on demand. A body over the inline limit comes back as a prefix, with both sizes and a pointer to `memory_search` for the rest.
tools.name: memory_read

name.description: Memory name as listed in the memory index.

tools.description: Find stored memories by content: case-insensitive substring match (no regex) over memory names and full text. Returns up to 10 memories with up to 3 matching lines each; 'total' counts every memory that matched, so when it exceeds what is shown, refine the query. Use memory_read for a hit's full text. Archived memories are not searched.

tools.description: Persist a named memory as a markdown file; reusing a name updates that memory, and 'created'/'updated' dates are stamped automatically. Names are slugs (letters, digits, '.', '_', '-'; max 128 chars). Every field follows one rule — omit it to keep what the memory has, pass it empty to remove it, pass a value to replace it — so a rewrite never drops what it does not mention. Frontmatter keys without a parameter of their own ride a leading `---` block in the text under the same rule, and text that is only such a block leaves the body as it is. If the result lists similar existing memories, update one of those instead of keeping a near-duplicate.
tools.name: memory_write

description.description: One-line summary shown in the memory index instead of the first body line. Omit to keep the current one, "" to remove it.

keywords.description: Comma-separated retrieval aliases — synonyms and cross-language equivalents (e.g. both English and Chinese terms) that should auto-recall this memory. Omit to keep the current ones, "" to remove them.

name.description: Slug-style memory name (letters, digits, '.', '_', '-'); reusing a name updates that memory.

related.description: Memory names, as the index lists them, that recall surfaces alongside this one when this memory is recalled. Omit to keep the current ones, [] to remove them.

text.description: Full memory body (markdown), replacing the body the memory has. Without a 'description' parameter, the first line becomes the index summary. Text that carries only a frontmatter fence keeps the existing body.

type.description: Memory category shown in the index. Omit to keep the current one, "" to remove it.

tools.description:
Activate a named skill so its instructions load into the current task.

## What it does

A single call activates ONE skill, chosen by the `skill` parameter from the
skill listing, with its arguments, if any, in `args` (what follows `/<name>`); its
instructions are in your context from your next step. A
listing line may be shortened to save context —
the skill behind it is complete, and activating it loads everything.

Make it the only tool call in its response. Batched with other tool calls,
those calls run but the skill is not loaded.

## When to use

- The task matches an available skill — activate it BEFORE producing other output
  about the task, so its guidance is in force while you work.
- The user references a skill by name or types `/<name>`.

## When NOT to use

- The skill you want is not in the listing — never guess or invent a name; pick
  only from the listed ones.
- A skill is already active — do not re-activate it.
- No listed skill covers the task — just proceed without one.
tools.name: skill

skill.description: Name of the skill to activate, from the skill listing in your context.
